Pascal
pas-KAL
proper noun (a French mathematician and apologist)
Blaise Pascal (1623-1662), the French mathematician, physicist, and Christian apologist of the Jansenist circle, author of the Pensées and the Provincial Letters.

📖 Biblical Definition

Blaise Pascal (1623-1662) was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, and Christian thinker of extraordinary genius, associated with the Jansenist circle of Port-Royal, whose religious writings—chiefly the Pensées (Thoughts) and the Provincial Letters—remain among the most penetrating in Christian literature. After a profound conversion experience in 1654, recorded on a parchment he sewed into his coat (the “Memorial”: “Fire. God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and scholars”), Pascal devoted his powers to the defence of the faith. The dictionary honours much in Pascal. He grasped, against the rationalism of his age, that the things of God are not reached by unaided reason but are spiritually discerned, for the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit; that God hides Himself from the wise and prudent and reveals Himself to babes; that the heart is deceitful above all and that man is at once wretched and great, a fallen creature made for God. His famous “wager” and his maxim that “the heart has its reasons which reason knows not” press the limits of mere intellect and the necessity of a God-given faith. The dictionary marks the cautions a Reformed reader must keep. Pascal was a Roman Catholic and a Jansenist, and his apologetic, for all its brilliance, is not free of his communion's errors; the wager, taken alone, can be mistaken for a prudential gamble rather than the venture of true faith. Yet read with discernment, Pascal is a profound witness to human depravity and divine grace, to the insufficiency of reason and the necessity of revelation—a brilliant mind brought low before the God of Abraham, not the god of the philosophers.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Blaise Pascal (1623-1662), French mathematician and Christian apologist of the Jansenist circle, author of the Pensées; honoured for his witness to human depravity, the limits of reason, and the necessity of grace, read with caution as a Roman Catholic Jansenist.

PASCAL, proper noun. Blaise Pascal (1623-1662), French mathematician, physicist, and Christian apologist.

Of the Jansenist circle of Port-Royal; author of the Pensées and Provincial Letters.

After a 1654 conversion he devoted his genius to the defence of the faith.

He grasped that the things of God are spiritually discerned, hidden from the wise (Matthew 11:25).

Read with caution as a Roman Catholic Jansenist, yet a profound witness to grace.

📖 Key Scripture

1 Co 1:25 — "Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men."

Jer 17:9 — "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?"

1 Co 2:14 — "But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned."

Mt 11:25 — "At that time Jesus answered and said, I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Pascal was a Roman Catholic Jansenist whose apologetic is not free of his communion's errors; his “wager,” taken alone, can be mistaken for a prudential gamble rather than the venture of true, God-given faith.

expand to see more

The dictionary honours much in Pascal. Against the proud rationalism of his age, he saw that the things of God are not scaled by unaided reason but spiritually discerned, that God hides Himself from the wise and prudent and reveals Himself to babes, that the human heart is deceitful above all and man at once wretched and great—a ruined creature made for God. His witness to human depravity, to the insufficiency of reason, and to the necessity of a faith God must give places him near the Reformed estimate of fallen man, and his religious genius has profited the church far beyond his own communion.

Yet the dictionary keeps the cautions a Reformed reader must. Pascal was a Roman Catholic and a Jansenist, and his thought, for all its brilliance, is not free of his communion's errors and ambiguities. His celebrated “wager,” isolated from the rest of his thought, can be misread as a cold prudential gamble—bet on God because the odds favour it—rather than the venture of a faith that God Himself works in the heart; true faith is not a calculation of self-interest but the gift of God. Read with discernment, however, Pascal remains a profound witness to the doctrines of grace, a towering intellect brought low before the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, not the god of the philosophers and scholars.

Blaise Pascal, French Pascal; his Pensées (“Thoughts”) and Lettres provinciales (“Provincial Letters”) are his chief religious works.
